title: Counting infinite sets
objectives: Show that the rationals are countable and, by the diagonal argument, the reals are not.

screens.title: Listing the integers
screens.prose: Can we list every integer, one after another, so that each gets a place? Try $0, 1, -1, 2, -2, 3, -3, \dots$: the arrows show the first steps.
screens.question: In this list, what position does $-3$ take?

hints.text: Continue the pattern past $-2$.
After $-2$ (5th) comes 3, then $-3$.
3 is 6th, so $-3$ is 7th.

feedback.correct: Right. In general $m$ is at position $2m$ and $-m$ at $2m + 1$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write the list out to $-3$ and count.

byKey.three: You gave the position of $+3$. $-3$ comes right after it.
byKey.neg: You gave the integer, not its place. Count along the list.
byKey.eight: You counted one too many. The list starts with 0 in place 1.

explain.text: The list runs 0, 1, $-1$, 2, $-2$, 3, $-3$, so $-3$ is 7th. Every integer gets one place: $m$ at $2m$, $-m$ at $2m + 1$. So $\mathbb{Z}$, which looks twice as big as $\mathbb{N}$, can be listed.

screens.title: Walking the fractions
screens.prose: Every positive fraction $\tfrac pq$ sits in this grid. Walk it diagonal by diagonal, $p + q = 2, 3, 4, \dots$, each starting at the top row. Skip any fraction not in lowest terms: it has appeared already.
screens.question: Tap the first six fractions of the walk, in order.

hints.text: $p + q = 2$ holds only $\tfrac11$. Then $p + q = 3$.
$p + q = 3$: $\tfrac12$, $\tfrac21$. $p + q = 4$: $\tfrac13$, $\tfrac22$, $\tfrac31$.
Skip $\tfrac22 = \tfrac11$. The sixth is $\tfrac14$, the top of $p + q = 5$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take one diagonal at a time, from the top row down, and skip repeats.

byKey.r2c2: You tapped $\tfrac22$. It equals $\tfrac11$, already listed, so the walk skips it.
byKey.order: Right fractions, wrong order. Each diagonal starts at the top row: $\tfrac12$ before $\tfrac21$.
byKey.r1c5: You jumped ahead to $\tfrac15$. Finish the diagonal $p + q = 5$ only after $\tfrac14$ starts it.

explain.text: The diagonals are finite, so the walk reaches each one. Skipping repeats such as $\tfrac22$ gives each fraction one place. So the positive rationals can be listed.

screens.title: Places in the walk
screens.prose: The walk has reached $\tfrac31$ in fifth place. Repeats are shaded. Keep walking along the diagonals.
screens.question: Fill in the positions of $\tfrac32$, $\tfrac23$ and $\tfrac15$.

hints.text: Diagonal $p + q = 5$ holds $\tfrac14, \tfrac23, \tfrac32, \tfrac41$, none repeated.
They take places 6, 7, 8, 9.
Diagonal $p + q = 6$ starts with $\tfrac15$: place 10.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Continue from $\tfrac31$ in place 5, skipping shaded cells.

byKey.r1c1: For $\tfrac23$: it is second on diagonal 5, after $\tfrac14$ in place 6.
byKey.r2c1: For $\tfrac15$: after $\tfrac41$ in place 9 comes diagonal 6, starting with $\tfrac15$. Counting $\tfrac22$ would give 11.

explain.text: Diagonal 5 fills places 6 to 9 with $\tfrac14, \tfrac23, \tfrac32, \tfrac41$. Diagonal 6 starts with $\tfrac15$ in place 10. Every fraction lands on a finite diagonal, so each has a place.

screens.title: Countable
screens.prose:
A set $A$ is **countable** when it can be listed: there is a function $f : \mathbb{N} \to A$ that is one-to-one and onto. For the integers,

$$f(2m) = m, \qquad f(2m + 1) = -m.$$

The walk gives such an $f$ for the positive rationals.
screens.question: Why must the walk skip $\tfrac22$?

options.text: $\tfrac22 = \tfrac11$: listing it again would give one number two places, so $f$ would not be one-to-one.

options.why: You ruled $\tfrac22$ out of the set. It is the positive rational 1.
You aimed for a shorter list. The list is infinite either way; skipping keeps each number to one place.

options.text: Fractions with even parts are left out.
options.why: You skipped by evenness. $\tfrac21$ has an even part and is listed in place 3.

hints.text: A list pairs each place with one number. What does a repeat break?
One-to-one: different places, different numbers.
$\tfrac22$ and $\tfrac11$ would be two places holding the number 1.

feedback.correct: Right. Each number gets exactly one place.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what a repeat does to the pairing of places with numbers.

explain.text: A bijection gives each number exactly one place. $\tfrac22$ is the number 1 again. Skipping it keeps $f$ one-to-one; onto holds because every fraction lies on some diagonal.

screens.title: Can $(0, 1)$ be listed?
screens.prose: Claim: the interval $(0, 1)$ is not countable. We prove it by contradiction. The proof is Cantor's diagonal argument.
screens.question: Which line starts the proof?

options.text: Suppose $(0, 1)$ is countable: a list $x_1, x_2, x_3, \dots$ contains every number in $(0, 1)$.

options.why: You supposed the claim. A contradiction proof supposes its opposite.
You fixed one list. Beating one list proves nothing; the proof must beat every list.
You negated the wrong thing. The opposite of not countable is countable, which includes infinite lists.

hints.text: What is the opposite of not countable?
Countable means some list contains every number.
The supposition names an arbitrary list, with letters.

feedback.correct: Right. Suppose an arbitrary complete list.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Suppose the opposite of the claim, for any list.

explain.text: The opposite of uncountable is countable: some list holds every number in $(0, 1)$. We call it $x_1, x_2, \dots$ without fixing it. Then we build a number it misses.

screens.title: Down the diagonal
screens.prose: Here is the start of a supposed list, to 5 places. Build $x$ digit by digit: its $k$th digit is 5, unless the $k$th digit of $x_k$ is 5; then it is 4.

state.caption: Digit $k$ of the $k$th number lies on the diagonal.

screens.question: Fill in the five diagonal digits, then the first five digits of $x$.

hints.text: The diagonal runs from row 1, digit 1, to row 5, digit 5.
Diagonal: 1, 1, 4, 5, 3.
Only the 4th is a 5, so $x = 0.55545\ldots$

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read digit $k$ of row $k$, then apply the rule.

byKey.r3c1: Digit 4 of $x_4 = 0.57751$ is 5. Read the fourth digit after the point.
byKey.r3c2: The 4th diagonal digit is 5, so the rule writes 4 there, not 5.

explain.text: The diagonal digits are 1, 1, 4, 5, 3. The rule writes 5 except under the 5, where it writes 4. So $x = 0.55545\ldots$, and digit $k$ of $x$ never matches digit $k$ of $x_k$.

screens.title: Missing from the list
screens.prose: In general, digit $k$ of $x$ differs from digit $k$ of $x_k$, for every $k$. Its digits are all 4s and 5s.
screens.question: Why is $x$ not in the list?

options.text: For each $k$, $x$ and $x_k$ differ in digit $k$, so $x \ne x_k$.

options.why: You put $x$ outside $(0, 1)$. It is between $0.4$ and $0.6$.
You checked one number. $x$ must differ from every $x_k$, and digit $k$ does that.

hints.text: Pick any $k$. Compare $x$ with $x_k$.
They disagree at digit $k$.
With digits only 4 and 5, $x$ has one decimal name, so disagreeing digits mean different numbers.

feedback.correct: Right. $x$ escapes every $x_k$ at its own digit.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find a reason that works for every $k$ at once.

explain.text: For any $k$, $x$ and $x_k$ disagree in digit $k$. So $x$ is none of the $x_k$. But $x \in (0, 1)$, so the list was not complete after all.

screens.title: The diagonal argument
screens.prose: Assemble the proof. Two lines are flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the two flawed lines to Left out.

lines.text: Suppose $(0, 1)$ is countable: a list $x_1, x_2, x_3, \dots$ holds every number in $(0, 1)$.
Write each $x_k$ in decimal, never ending in an unbroken run of 9s.
Let $x$ have $k$th digit 5, unless the $k$th digit of $x_k$ is 5; then 4.
$x \in (0, 1)$, and with only 4s and 5s it has one decimal name.
For each $k$, $x$ and $x_k$ differ in digit $k$, so $x \ne x_k$.
So $x$ is missing from the list, a contradiction: $(0, 1)$ is uncountable. $\blacksquare$
Let $x$ have $k$th digit one more than the $k$th digit of $x_k$.
lines.why: You add 1 to each digit. A 9 has no next digit, and the 0s and 9s this makes allow two decimal names.
You claimed $x$ is irrational. The proof never shows it, and does not need it.

hints.text: Suppose a list, fix decimal names, build $x$, compare.
The line about one decimal name comes just after $x$ is built.
Order: suppose, decimals, build $x$, $x \in (0, 1)$, differs from each $x_k$, contradiction.

feedback.correct: Right. No list of $(0, 1)$ is complete, so $(0, 1)$ is uncountable.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Build $x$ before comparing it with the list.

byKey.d1: You used the add-one rule. It turns 9 into 10 and can make 0s and 9s; the 5 and 4 rule avoids both.
byKey.d2: You used the line calling $x$ irrational. Nothing shows it, and the contradiction does not need it.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the two flawed lines go to Left out.

explain.text: Any list of $(0, 1)$ misses the diagonal number $x$. So no list is complete. The reals in $(0, 1)$, and so $\mathbb{R}$, are uncountable.

screens.title: The rationals are uncountable?
screens.prose: A classmate runs the diagonal argument on a list of the rationals in $(0, 1)$. But the walk showed those rationals are countable, so some line must be broken.

rows: Suppose the rationals in $(0, 1)$ are listed: $r_1, r_2, r_3, \dots$
Build $x$ with 5s and 4s, changing digit $k$ of $r_k$.
$x$ is a rational in $(0, 1)$, so it must be some $r_k$.
Contradiction: the rationals in $(0, 1)$ are uncountable.

screens.question: Tap the line that does not follow.

hints.text: Which line claims something about $x$ that was never shown?
Lines 2 and 3 are the usual construction.
Nothing shows $x$ is rational, and for many lists it is not.

feedback.correct: Right. $x$ need not be rational, so it need not be on the list.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the line that asserts something never proved.

byKey.r1: Line 2 is the usual construction. It works on any list.
byKey.r2: Line 3 is fine: $x$ differs from $r_k$ in digit $k$.
byKey.r4: Line 5 would follow from line 4. The fault is that line 4 assumes $x$ is rational.
byKey.r0: Line 1 is a fair supposition, and in fact true.

explain.text: The diagonal number escapes the list, but nothing makes it rational. So line 4 fails, and no contradiction follows. For $(0, 1)$ itself, $x$ is automatically in the set, which is why the argument works there.

screens.title: Why 5s and 4s?
screens.prose: The rule writes only 5s and 4s. A simpler-looking rule, changing each digit to 0 or 9, can fail, because $0.4999\ldots = 0.5$.
screens.question: What goes wrong with digits 0 and 9?

options.text: A number can have two decimal names, so a different digit need not mean a different number.
0 and 9 are not allowed as digits of numbers in $(0, 1)$.
options.why: You banned 0 and 9. $0.09$ and $0.9$ are in $(0, 1)$.
You worried about size. Size is not the issue; $x = 0.0909\ldots$ is still in $(0, 1)$.
You picked on 9 being odd. 5 is odd too, and it is fine.

hints.text: Compute $0.4999\ldots$ as a series.
So $0.4999\ldots$ and $0.5000\ldots$ are one number with two names.

feedback.correct: Right. With only 4s and 5s, $x$ has one name, so a differing digit means a different number.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about $0.4999\ldots$ and $0.5$.

explain.text: $0.4999\ldots = 0.4 + \tfrac{0.09}{1 - 0.1} = 0.5$. If $x$ ended in 9s, it could equal some $x_k$ written with 0s. A name using only 4s and 5s is the number's only name.

screens.title: The walk as code
screens.prose: Write `rational_at(k)`, the $k$th fraction of the walk as a `Fraction`, and `index_of(p, q)`, the position of $\tfrac pq$. Cancel $\tfrac pq$ first: $\tfrac24$ sits where $\tfrac12$ does.
screens.question: Complete both functions.

widget.starter:
from fractions import Fraction
from math import gcd

def rational_at(k):
    """The k-th positive rational (k = 1, 2, ...) in the walk."""
    ...

def index_of(p, q):
    """The position of p/q in the walk (p, q >= 1)."""
    ...

tests.call: all(index_of(rational_at(k).numerator, rational_at(k).denominator) == k for k in range(1, 101))

widget.how: Check runs 12 hidden tests. Six call rational_at, which must return a Fraction. Five call index_of, one on a fraction not in lowest terms. The last is a round trip over the first 100 places.

hints.text: Loop over diagonals $s = p + q = 2, 3, 4, \dots$ and $p = 1$ to $s - 1$.
Count only fractions with $\gcd(p, s - p) = 1$.
`index_of`: cancel by the gcd first. Count the whole diagonals before $p + q$. Then count lowest-terms fractions up to $p$ on its own diagonal.

feedback.correct: Right. The walk and its inverse agree on the first 100 places.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Skip fractions whose gcd is above 1, and cancel the input of `index_of`.

explain.text: `rational_at` walks the diagonals and counts only lowest-terms fractions. `index_of` counts the same fractions up to $\tfrac pq$. The round trip is the bijection with $\mathbb{N}$ checked on 100 places.

screens.title: Strategies you can write down
screens.prose: Every coded trading strategy is a finite string of characters. A strategy in general is any rule from price histories to positions. The diagonal argument shows there are uncountably many such rules.
screens.question: Which statement is true?

options.text: Coded strategies are countable: list them by length, then alphabetically. So almost no rule can be coded.
Coded strategies are uncountable, because there are infinitely many.
options.why: You equated infinite with uncountable. $\mathbb{N}$ is infinite and countable.

options.text: Every rule from price histories to positions can be coded.
options.why: You assumed every rule has a program. Programs are countable and rules are not, so most rules have none.

options.text: There are only finitely many coded strategies.
options.why: You capped program length. Programs of every length exist, so the list is infinite.

hints.text: Strings of a fixed length are finitely many.
List all strings of length 1, then length 2, and so on.
That list is countable; the set of all rules is not, so most rules have no program.

feedback.correct: Right. Countably many programs, uncountably many rules.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the programs can be put in a list.

explain.text: Each length gives a finite batch of strings, so listing batch after batch counts every program. Rules from histories to positions are uncountable. So the strategies a desk can code are a countable sliver of all possible rules.

ideas: Countable means listable: a one-to-one, onto $f : \mathbb{N} \to A$. $\mathbb{Z}$ alternates signs; $\mathbb{Q}$ walks diagonals.
Diagonal argument: from any list of $(0, 1)$, build $x$ whose digit $k$ differs from digit $k$ of $x_k$. $x$ is missing, so $(0, 1)$ is uncountable.
Use only 5s and 4s: $0.4999\ldots = 0.5$, so 0s and 9s allow two names for one number.

formula.name: Integers listed
formula.note: A bijection with $\mathbb{N}$ is a list: each element gets exactly one place.

summary.trap: The diagonal argument on a list of rationals proves nothing: the new number need not be rational.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. List the integers up to 4.

byKey.nine: You gave the place of $-4$. 4 comes just before it.

quiz.prose: The walk lists $\tfrac pq$ diagonal by diagonal, $p + q = 2, 3, \dots$, top row first, skipping fractions not in lowest terms. $\tfrac15$ is 10th and $\tfrac51$ is 11th.
quiz.question: What position does $\tfrac16$ take?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Diagonal 6 is $\tfrac15$ and $\tfrac51$ once repeats are skipped.

byKey.repeat: You counted the repeats $\tfrac22$, $\tfrac24$, $\tfrac33$ and $\tfrac42$. The walk skips them.
byKey.diag: You gave the place of $\tfrac51$, which ends diagonal 6. $\tfrac16$ comes next.

explain.text: Diagonals 2 to 6 hold $1 + 2 + 2 + 4 + 2 = 11$ lowest-terms fractions. $\tfrac16$ opens diagonal 7. So it is 12th.

quiz.prose: Some infinite sets can be listed and some cannot.
quiz.question: Which sets are countable? Select all that apply.

options.why: You called $(0, 1)$ countable. The diagonal argument beats every list of it.
You called $\mathbb{R}$ countable. It contains $(0, 1)$, which is not.

feedback.correct: Right. $\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathbb{Q}$ and the strings can be listed.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether each set has a list that reaches every element.

explain.text: $\mathbb{Z}$ alternates signs, $\mathbb{Q}$ walks diagonals with signs, and strings go by length. $(0, 1)$ escapes every list by the diagonal argument, and so does $\mathbb{R} \supseteq (0, 1)$.

quiz.prose: A list begins $x_1 = 0.25000\ldots$, $x_2 = 0.55500\ldots$, $x_3 = 0.12300\ldots$ Use the rule: digit 5, unless the diagonal digit is 5, then 4.
quiz.question: What are the first three digits of $x$? Type them as $0.d_1d_2d_3$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The diagonal digits are 2, 5 and 3.

byKey.copy: You copied the diagonal digits. The rule changes each of them.
byKey.all5: You wrote 5 everywhere. Digit 2 of $x_2$ is 5, so the rule writes 4 there.

explain.text: The diagonal digits are 2, 5, 3. The rule gives 5, 4, 5. So $x = 0.545\ldots$ differs from each $x_k$ in digit $k$.
